claims.text: The starting catalyst is a multi-element automotive alloy containing multiple principal elements in nearly equiatomic ratios.
The untreated starting catalyst exhibits activity loss and durability limitations during transient and low-temperature exhaust operation.
An ultrathin, nanometer-scale high-entropy oxide coating can be deposited conformally on the catalyst particles by atomic layer deposition.
A coating containing multiple rare-earth or transition-metal cations can enhance thermal stability.
A coating containing selected rare-earth or transition-metal cations can enhance oxygen mobility.
The high-entropy oxide coating can remain oxygen-permeable without hindering the catalyst's active surface sites.
The deposited high-entropy oxide forms a conformal nanoscale barrier on the catalyst surface.
The oxide barrier suppresses thermally induced agglomeration and sintering of active catalyst particles.
The oxide coating moderates adsorption of deactivating species such as H2O and NO.
Moderating H2O and NO adsorption suppresses surface poisoning.
The coating maintains active interfacial sites for oxygen exchange.
The coating stabilizes the catalyst microstructure during thermal excursions.
Compared with the untreated catalyst, the coated catalyst will have a lower deactivation rate under transient, low-temperature exhaust conditions.
Compared with the untreated catalyst, the coated catalyst will retain catalytic activity over extended operating cycles involving H2O, NO, and thermal aging.
The coating intervention preserves low platinum-group-metal consumption because it does not require increasing PGM loading.
High-entropy oxide coatings have shown promise in catalyst systems related to the proposed multi-element alloy catalyst.
